title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers actually revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before it is sent to students. Rather than evaluating AI feedback in isolation, the study asks three questions: what textual features are associated with teacher revisions, whether revision decisions can be predicted from the AI-generated text alone, and how revisions change the pedagogical type of feedback. The core problem is that teachers act as gatekeepers in AI-supported feedback systems, so the educational impact of generative AI depends not just on model output quality but on how educators accept, edit, or reshape that output.

The authors analyze log data from Tutoria, an AI-supported feedback platform integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom. In the platform, an LLM generates draft feedback for short open-ended student responses, and teachers can accept, edit, or rewrite it before delivery. The dataset contains 1,349 AI-generated feedback instances and corresponding final teacher-delivered messages from 117 teachers. Quantitatively, the study uses descriptive statistics, semantic similarity measures, and predictive modeling to analyze revision behavior. Qualitatively, it applies theory-informed coding to classify feedback as corrective, high-information, reinforcement/punishment, or other, enabling analysis of how teachers reshape the pedagogical character of the feedback.

The population and context span multiple Brazilian educational settings, including high school chemistry classes and undergraduate computer science contexts, along with additional extracurricular computing-related settings. Teachers were the main focal users, though students were the recipients of the feedback. Across all instances, teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in about 78% of cases, and roughly half of teachers never edited any AI-generated feedback. When edits did occur, they usually shortened the feedback while preserving most semantic content. Teacher editing behavior varied substantially across individuals.

The main conclusion is that teacher mediation of AI feedback is selective rather than constant. Default AI behavior matters because most feedback is passed on unchanged. When teachers do intervene, they often simplify verbose, high-information explanations into more concise corrective forms, suggesting that AI-generated feedback may frequently overscaffold or misalign with teacher priorities. Predictive models using only feedback text achieved modest above-chance performance in identifying which messages would be revised, indicating that revision depends partly on the text itself but also on contextual and teacher-specific factors not captured in the models. Overall, the paper argues that AI feedback should be evaluated as a co-created artifact shaped through teacher-AI interaction, not just as raw model output.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical observational/log-analysis study with quantitative and qualitative coding, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experiment and does not estimate causal effects on student learning. It provides direct classroom-process evidence on teacher mediation of LLM feedback, with clear methods but limited causal credibility.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows potentially useful operational benefits and significant shifts in feedback form, but impacts on student outcomes are unclear and no direct literacy effect sizes are reported. Thus the practical impact is modest or uncertain rather than clearly positive on learner achievement.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated formative feedback drafts for short open-ended student responses in a classroom platform, with teachers accepting, editing, or rewriting feedback before delivery.
Generative-AI-supported educational writing feedback, including teacher mediation of feedback language, explanatory density, and corrective wording for student-written responses.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that teachers accepted AI-generated feedback without modification in 77.8% of 1,349 cases, suggesting the system often reduced editing effort. However, editing behavior was heterogeneous across 117 teachers: about 51.3% edited at least once, roughly half edited fewer than 6% of messages, and the top decile revised about two-thirds; text-only prediction of revisions achieved modest performance (AUC up to 0.75), indicating some ability to anticipate where human effort will be needed.
finding.measure: Teacher acceptance/edit rates, feedback length differences, cosine similarity between AI and final feedback, and prediction metrics for revision decisions (AUC, balanced accuracy, Cohen's kappa)
finding.effect_size: AUC=0.75; Cohen's kappa up to 0.387; within-teacher Wilcoxon W=460.5, p=.024 for length difference
finding.std_deviation: AI feedback length SD=19.60; final feedback length SD=19.81; similarity SD=0.09

finding.finding_summary: This paper examines literacy-related feedback processes around student written short responses, but it does not measure student literacy learning gains directly. Qualitative coding of 834 deduplicated messages showed that unrevised feedback was more often corrective (58.1%) than high-information (41.9%), while revised cases started more often as high-information (59.9%) and shifted after teacher editing toward more concise corrective or other forms; the pre/post shift was statistically significant but small (chi-square=4.55, p=.033, Cramer's V=0.12).
finding.measure: Pedagogical feedback-type coding of AI-generated versus teacher-revised written feedback messages
finding.study_size: n=834 deduplicated feedback messages coded; full log n=1349 instances
finding.effect_size: Cramer's V=0.12; Cohen's w=0.16 to 0.20 for distributional differences
